responses.response: Use the shared deployment kinds and keep the nesting strict: production environment, zones inside it, one infrastructure node per deployable responsibility named Environment plus Service plus Vm, and one Node_App inside each VM. Link each deployed app to the logical model with instanceOf pointing to the container FQN from the system model. Do not copy normal deployment relationships manually because LikeC4 inherits them automatically through instanceOf. Put technologies such as HTTPS or database ports on the logical system-model relationships, not on duplicated deployment edges. Add deployment relationships only for infrastructure-specific flows such as monitoring, backups, bastion access, log shipping, or replication. Also give each VM a rich Markdown description table with network interface first, then OS, CPU, RAM, port, and RTO; zone descriptions should carry VLAN, CIDR, and firewall context.

Use this skill for the base deployment shape and naming, but switch to structure-deployment-tiers for the detailed Dmz, AppTier, ProcTier, and DataTier split and the firewall rules between zones. Stay here for environment to zone to infrastructure node to Node_App, naming, descriptions, and instanceOf. Switch there when the main problem is inter-zone structure, tier semantics, and firewall rule documentation.

Do not invent worker VMs or host specs you do not actually know. The shared deployment spec includes Node_Cluster, so the honest managed-Kubernetes shape is: a production environment, a truthful platform zone, a Node_Cluster for the managed Kubernetes runtime, and Node_App instances under that cluster, each linked with instanceOf. If MongoDB runs outside the cluster, place it under its own honest infrastructure node in the appropriate zone; if it is a managed external service, model it as such rather than pretending it sits on a VM you control. The key is to model the platform boundary you actually know, not fake physical hosts.

No. Those technologies usually belong on the logical relationships in the system model, not on duplicated deployment edges for normal application traffic. Once deployed apps use instanceOf, LikeC4 inherits the relationships automatically into deployment views. Even though the shared deployment spec defines deployment relationship kinds like https and tcp, use them sparingly for infrastructure-specific connections that are not part of normal business traffic, such as monitoring, backups, bastion access, log shipping, or replication.

Add the Prometheus scrape if Prometheus is an operational or infrastructure actor that is not already represented by an inherited logical relationship. Monitoring traffic is exactly the kind of deployment-specific edge worth modeling. Good candidates to add in deployment are Prometheus scraping the API VM or Node_App, backup agents writing to backup storage, bastion or admin access, log shipping or SIEM forwarding, and database replication. Avoid duplicating anything that already exists in the logical model and will be inherited through instanceOf, especially browser to API traffic, API to service calls, or service to database calls.
